name: Andes
title: The Organizer
pitch: Unite a hundred quarrelling valleys by making them all richer together.

core.n: Lupaca shore of Lake Titicaca (later Chucuito)
core.d: The most crowded, richest highland basin of the time: the biggest herds, lake fish, reeds, potatoes and quinoa, with Tiwanaku's raised fields waiting to be revived. Copper and tin are within a few hundred km.

img.cap: Lake Titicaca from the hills above Chucuito

start.d: He arrives in the hills above the west shore, near the Lupaca hilltop seat at Cutimbo (about 3,900 m), and quarantines alone for about 3 weeks before meeting anyone.

img.cap: Lupaca burial towers on the Cutimbo hilltop

facts: Cold high plateau: sunny days, freezing nights most of the year; thin air
~600–800 mm at the lake, nearly all Dec–Mar; drier to the south (~300 mm at Oruro)
~Oct–Apr; frost can strike any month, so one bad night can kill a crop
Aymara at the lake, Puquina and Uruquilla in pockets; Quechua dialects to the north
None. Quipu knotted cords record numbers in base 10
Llama, alpaca, guinea pig, dog. No draft animals; a llama carries ~25–35 kg
Copper, arsenical and tin bronze, gold, silver. No iron

land.d: 8,300 km² of slightly salty fresh water that softens frost along its shores. Fish, reeds and waterbirds; reed boats are the only transport across it.

img.cap: Lake Titicaca: islands, bays and dry shore hills

land.d: Flat, crowded farmland of potatoes, quinoa and cañihua, with relic raised fields along the shore. No malaria; the danger is frost and drought.

img.cap: Quinoa drying in lakeside fields near Puno

land.d: Wide grassy plains and river flats north-west of the lake. Rich pasture and large raised-field zones; Colla country.

img.cap: Grassy shores of Lake Umayo in Colla country

land.d: Treeless ichu-grass and wetland (bofedal) pasture, too cold for crops. Llama and alpaca herds; fuel is dung and yareta moss.

img.c: Photo: Pedro Nolberto Flores Mamani, CC BY-SA 4.0
img.cap: Llamas and alpacas on ichu-grass puna in Puno

land.d: A glacier wall east of the lake (Illampu, Illimani). Glacier melt feeds streams for water wheels later; passes lead down to the Yungas.

img.cap: The Illampu glaciers rising beyond Lake Titicaca

land.d: Steep cloud forest with coca, fruit, timber and cinchona bark. Leishmaniasis and some malaria low down; landslides.

img.cap: Steep cloud-forest valleys of the Yungas near Coroico

land.d: A drier, harsher plain of herders. The Desaguadero river drains Titicaca into shallow, salty Lake Poopó. Tin and copper country.

img.c: Photo: Diego Calderón Acebey, CC BY-SA 4.0
img.cap: Bofedal wetland pasture with herds below Sajama

land.d: Bare desert cut by green river oases where maize, cotton, peppers and fruit grow. The Lupaca kept farming colonies here; 2–4 days' walk from the lake.

img.cap: Green Moquegua oasis below the bare desert of Cerro Baúl

land.d: The La Raya pass (4,300 m) leads down a long Quechua farming valley to Cusco. Lower and warmer, so maize grows; the natural road north.

img.cap: Wide grassy valley at the La Raya pass

land.n: Salt flats of the far south (Coipasa, Uyuni)
land.d: The world's largest salt flats on a dry, windy plain. Unlimited salt, little else; very thin population.

img.c: Photo: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag), edit by Trialsanderrors, CC BY-SA 2.5
img.cap: Salt piles cut from the crust of the Salar de Uyuni

peoples.popText: ~60,000–100,000 (guess); the last Inca census counted ~20,000 households (~100,000 people) in 1532
peoples.culture: Aymara herding and farming lords, seat at Cutimbo; ayllu kin groups, two halves (upper and lower) each with its lord. Huge herds, colonies down on the coast
peoples.d: His hosts. Big, rich and organized, but at war with the Colla. A Lupaca lord is his route to power.

peoples.culture: Aymara lords centred on Hatuncolla, chullpa burial towers at Sillustani; herders and raised-field farmers
peoples.d: Bitter rivals of the Lupaca. The second big prize; he brings them in with membership, not war.

img.cap: Colla chullpa burial towers at Sillustani

peoples.popText: ~10,000–25,000 (guess; ~4,000 Uru households in the Inca count for Chucuito)
peoples.culture: Fishers, fowlers and reed-gatherers speaking Uruquilla/Puquina; live on the shore and on reed islands; low status, few herds
peoples.d: The lake's experts in boats, fish and reeds. Treated as poor outsiders by the Aymara, so fair treatment wins them fast.

img.cap: Reed islands and totora boats of the Uru

peoples.culture: Aymara lordship south-east of the lake around Caquiaviri and the old Tiwanaku lands; herders and farmers
peoples.d: Hold the Tiwanaku ruins and the Corocoro copper. A natural early member of the network.

peoples.culture: Aymara lordships around Achacachi on the north-east shore, under the Cordillera Real
peoples.d: Control the passes down to the Yungas (coca, timber, fruit).

peoples.culture: Herders and farmers of the upper Vilcanota, between the lake and Cusco; Quechua- and Aymara-speaking
peoples.d: The bridge to Cusco. Whoever has them controls the road north.

peoples.culture: Aymara/Puquina-speaking terrace farmers and herders in the deep Colca canyon; famous terraces
peoples.d: Expert terrace builders, with the Chivay obsidian source next door.

img.c: Photo: Dr. Eugen Lehle, CC BY-SA 3.0
img.cap: Old farming terraces along the Colca valley

peoples.culture: Aymara herding lordships of the dry southern altiplano down to Potosí and Sucre
peoples.d: Live on the tin belt and near the salt flats. Hit hardest by drought, so they need storehouse insurance most.

peoples.popText: ~20,000–40,000 in the valley (guess); the capital covered ~50 ha
peoples.culture: Quechua-speaking farmers; a small, ambitious royal lineage (legendary kings Sinchi Roca or Lloque Yupanqui around now); maize, terraces
peoples.d: A minor kingdom in 1230, not yet an empire. A young Inca prince could become his student, or his future rival.

img.cap: Sacsayhuamán walls above Cusco, finished by later Inca

peoples.culture: Warlike Quechua-speaking confederation around Andahuaylas and Ayacucho; hilltop forts, ancestor mummies carried into battle
peoples.d: The strongest highland military power west of Cusco; in real history nearly took Cusco around 1438.

peoples.popText: ~100,000–200,000 (guess; the valley was densely packed with hilltop towns)
peoples.culture: Quechua-speaking farmers in the broad, fertile Mantaro valley; feuding fortified towns, no single ruler
peoples.d: One of the densest farming valleys in the Andes; near the Cerro de Pasco silver. A rich prize later.

peoples.popText: ~30,000 in Chan Chan; ~300,000–500,000 in the kingdom (guess)
peoples.culture: The one true state: divine king, nobles, huge irrigation canals, master metalworkers and weavers; Muchik language; sea worship
peoples.d: The coast partner he most needs: they sit next to the only Andean coal and have sea transport.

img.cap: Seabird reliefs on Chan Chan's adobe walls

peoples.culture: North-coast lords of the Batán Grande area; the Andes' biggest arsenical-bronze industry; declining after a flood and fire around 1100
peoples.d: Bronze smelting know-how at scale. The Chimú will absorb them in the 1300s.

peoples.culture: Highland farmers in a broad northern valley; fine kaolin pottery; trade with the Chimú coast
peoples.d: Gateway between the north highlands and Chimú. Close to the northern coalfield.

peoples.popText: ~50,000–100,000 (guess); a Spanish report later counted 30,000 tribute-payers incl. 10,000 fishermen and 6,000 merchants
peoples.culture: Seafaring trader-lords of the south-central coast; balsa rafts, sea trade as far as Ecuador; guano-fertilized fields
peoples.d: The great traders and sailors. They control the guano islands offshore.

img.cap: Huaca La Centinela, the Chincha lords' seat

peoples.culture: Desert-oasis farmers and potters (Ica culture); cotton, maize, irrigation
peoples.d: Cotton and oasis food, a day or two from the Marcona iron coast.

peoples.culture: Oasis farmers and fishers of the Azapa and Lluta valleys (Arica culture); trade with the altiplano
peoples.d: The lake's nearest sea outlet to the south-west; fish, seaweed, cotton and guano.

peoples.culture: Oasis farmers and llama caravan traders around San Pedro de Atacama; copper workers; Kunza language. On the coast, Chango fishers hunt sea lions from sealskin floats
peoples.d: Know the deserts, copper and salt routes south. Small, but key guides to the nitrates.

peoples.culture: Lowland farmers who built raised fields, causeways, canals and fish weirs on seasonally flooded savanna; Arawak-speaking groups
peoples.d: Proof that lowland peoples build big earthworks. Rubber, cacao and fish; malaria country.

peoples.culture: Small village groups of Arawak and Pano speakers along the Madre de Dios and Beni rivers; hunting, fishing, manioc
peoples.d: Trade feathers, wood and medicines up to the highlands. Independent and hard to reach.

resources.qty: modern: ~1.46 million alpacas in Puno region alone (2017), Peru ~3.7 million; Bolivia holds ~65% of the world's llamas
resources.reach: 1230: hundreds of thousands of animals in the basin (guess); great lords own thousands each. Wool, meat, dung fuel and pack transport
resources.d: The region's real wealth. Llamas carry but cannot plough; alpacas give the best wool.

resources.qty: modern: ~80,000+ ha of old raised fields mapped around the lake (estimate, ~)
resources.reach: 1230: mostly abandoned since Tiwanaku fell; rebuildable with spades and mit'a labor. Trials in the 1980s gave several times normal potato yields in frost years
resources.d: His first big proof. The water channels hold heat and protect crops from frost.

resources.qty: modern: Puno is a top potato and quinoa region of Peru
resources.reach: 1230: hundreds of potato varieties already grown; freeze-dried chuño keeps for years
resources.d: Staple food. Frost-tolerant bitter potatoes grow up to ~4,200 m.

resources.qty: modern: native killifish (carachi) and catfish (suche, mauri); a few thousand t a year (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: Uru fishers with reed boats and nets; dried and salted fish
resources.d: Steady protein. No trout yet (that was introduced in the 1940s).

resources.qty: modern: tens of thousands of ha of reed beds in the lake (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: cut by hand from shore and boats; boats, mats, roofing, floating islands, animal fodder
resources.d: The lake's timber substitute. Edible shoots too.

resources.qty: modern: ~893 km³; salinity ~1 g/L (drinkable but brackish)
resources.reach: 1230: unlimited for herds and irrigation; streams from the hills are better for drinking
resources.d: Steady water and a frost buffer. Boil before drinking near villages.

resources.qty: modern: sandstone-hosted copper, much of it native metal; mined since pre-Inca times; large resource (exact size unknown)
resources.reach: 1230: native copper and green ore at the surface; pick it out and hammer or smelt in wind-blown furnaces (huayra)
resources.d: The closest big copper to the lake, in Pacajes land. Bronze and, much later, wire.

resources.qty: modern: part of the Bolivian tin belt; Huanuni nearby made ~8,400 t of tin in 2017, Bolivia's largest mine
resources.reach: 1230: cassiterite (tin stone) in stream gravels and outcrops; wash it from gravel and smelt with copper for tin bronze
resources.d: Tin makes bronze much harder than copper. The key metal for his tools.

resources.qty: modern: tens of thousands of cut andesite and sandstone blocks, some over 100 t
resources.reach: 1230: lying in the open; ready-cut stone and proof of a past great state
resources.d: A source of prestige as much as stone. He frames his ideas as reviving Tiwanaku.

resources.qty: modern: large andesite and sandstone quarry zones that supplied Tiwanaku
resources.reach: 1230: open quarries; blocks move by reed boat across the lake
resources.d: Good building stone close to water transport.

resources.qty: modern: limestone beds around Pucará and Juliaca (size not checked)
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops; burn in pit kilns for lime mortar and plaster (fuel is the problem)
resources.d: Lime for mortar, plaster and later concrete.

resources.qty: modern: widespread lake-bed and river clays
resources.reach: 1230: dug everywhere; Pucará and Tiwanaku potters were famous
resources.d: Bricks, storage jars, kilns and molds for casting bronze.

resources.n: Fuel: dung, yareta and bofedal peat
resources.qty: modern: no woods; peat in high wetlands; yareta cushion plants grow ~1 cm a year
resources.reach: 1230: llama dung (taquia) is the main fuel; yareta and ichu grass too
resources.d: Fuel is the basin's worst shortage. Smelting must go where fuel is, or use charcoal from the valleys.

resources.qty: modern: small scattered groves; once much wider
resources.reach: 1230: patches on sheltered slopes; poles and fuel, easily overcut
resources.d: The only highland trees. Must be protected and replanted.

resources.qty: modern: rich alluvial gold districts (Sandia, Carabaya); large but uncounted
resources.reach: 1230: river gravels washed by hand on the forest edge
resources.d: Gold for gifts and status, not tools. A useful trade card.

resources.qty: modern: sulfur deposits mined in the 1900s
resources.reach: 1230: yellow sulfur crusts at the summit vents (~5,000 m)
resources.d: Later for sulfuric acid, blasting powder and rubber vulcanizing.

resources.qty: modern: the main obsidian source of the south-central Andes
resources.reach: 1230: quarried at the surface; sharp blades and scalpel-grade edges
resources.d: Razor blades for surgery and craft until bronze and iron take over.

resources.qty: modern: a few thousand ha of irrigated valley land
resources.reach: 1230: Lupaca colonies already farm maize, peppers, cotton and fruit here
resources.d: The lake's lowland larder, a few days down the slope.

resources.qty: modern: the main Bolivian coca and fruit zone
resources.reach: 1230: steep paths from the east shore; coca leaf, maize, fruit, hardwood, cinchona bark
resources.d: Warm-valley goods and real timber. Coca eases altitude and hunger.

resources.qty: modern: two giant porphyry copper mines, billions of t of ore at ~0.5–0.7% Cu
resources.reach: 1230: green-stained outcrops only; too low-grade to use well without modern methods
resources.d: Huge for the future, little use now. Mostly a 1300s-plus resource.

nearby.qty: modern: the richest silver hill ever; ~30,000–60,000 t of silver mined since 1545; early ores 4% silver on average, some up to 40%
nearby.reach: 1230: not yet worked (found by the Inca or Spanish later); rich oxidized ores at the surface
nearby.d: A trade fortune if he points people to it. Tim cares more about practical metals, so it is a later card.

nearby.qty: modern: the heart of the Bolivian tin belt; Huanuni makes over half of Bolivia's tin
nearby.reach: 1230: cassiterite in outcrops and stream gravels
nearby.d: The biggest tin supply for large-scale bronze.

nearby.qty: modern: ~10,000 km², ~10 billion t of salt
nearby.reach: 1230: cut as blocks from the crust and carried out by llama caravan
nearby.d: Unlimited salt for preserving food and for health. Iodine still has to come from the sea.

nearby.reach: 1230: crust salt cut by hand, a little closer than Uyuni

nearby.qty: modern: Peru's anchoveta catch 6–9 million t a year, up to ~12 million t (1970); the Humboldt system gives ~18–20% of the world's sea catch
nearby.reach: 1230: reed boats and nets near shore; dry and salt the fish, carry it up by llama
nearby.d: The richest fishery on Earth, a few days from the lake. Collapses in El Niño years.

nearby.qty: modern: abundant kelp along the south coast
nearby.reach: 1230: gathered on the shore and dried
nearby.d: The fix for goiter in the highlands.

nearby.qty: modern: the world's only big natural nitrate beds; caliche holds ~5–30% nitrate; mined at ~1 million t a year for decades
nearby.reach: 1230: caliche crust a few metres under the desert surface; dig and leach with hot water
nearby.d: Fertilizer and the oxidizer for blasting powder (roads and mines).

nearby.qty: modern: one of the largest copper deposits on Earth; billions of t of ore
nearby.reach: 1230: worked on a small scale by Atacama peoples; rich green surface ores
nearby.d: The long-term copper giant of the south.

nearby.qty: modern: ~1.4 billion t of magnetite ore at ~54% Fe (2012 estimate); the best bodies average 57–58% Fe
nearby.reach: 1230: black magnetite outcrops right on the desert coast; no fuel nearby
nearby.d: The Andes' best iron, but far from coal. Moves by raft to a smelter at the coal.

nearby.qty: modern: piles up to ~50 m (160–180 ft) deep in the 1840s; Peru shipped ~11–12 million t of guano in 1840–1880
nearby.reach: 1230: dug with digging sticks, rafted to shore by the Chincha; it can double or triple yields
nearby.d: The best fertilizer on Earth. The Chincha already use it, so it comes through trade.

nearby.n: Santa valley and Alto Chicama coal
nearby.qty: modern: Peru's largest coalfield (mostly anthracite), ~200 km long from the Chicama to the Santa river; Peru has ~1 billion t of coal reserves in all
nearby.reach: 1230: seams outcrop in the canyon walls; the Chimú may have burned some (coal ash at Chan Chan, 2004 study)
nearby.d: The only real coal in the Andes. Where the first iron smelter goes, with the Chimú as partners.

nearby.n: Cerro de Pasco silver, lead and zinc
nearby.qty: modern: a giant silver-zinc-lead-copper district; tailings piles alone hold ~70+ million t at ~44 g/t silver
nearby.reach: 1230: oxidized silver ores at the surface at ~4,300 m; small pre-Inca workings
nearby.d: Lead for pipes and type metal, zinc for brass and batteries, silver for trade.

nearby.reach: 1230: native cotton grown in irrigated oases, including brown and white kinds
nearby.d: Cloth and rag paper. Comes by trade with the coast.

nearby.qty: modern: wild cinchona trees on the eastern slopes; wild rubber trees in Madre de Dios
nearby.reach: 1230: forest gathering by lowland peoples; quinine is not yet known as a medicine
nearby.d: Quinine against malaria, rubber for seals and belts.

nearby.qty: modern: ~3,000–5,000 small evaporation pans fed by a salty spring
nearby.reach: 1230: already worked by hand near Cusco
nearby.d: Salt on the road to Cusco.

newcomers.d: Whole valleys sign up for storehouse insurance after a bad frost year. Same language, gods and ayllu ways, so they fit almost perfectly.
Same culture but bitter rivals. They join as members with their own lords, and the old feud is the risk.

newcomers.n: Drought refugees from the southern altiplano
newcomers.d: Carangas, Killaka and Lipez herders whose pastures fail. Aymara herders like the Lupaca; settled spread through ayllus, not in camps.

newcomers.when: every few decades; strong events roughly 1–3 times a century
newcomers.d: Fishers and oasis farmers whose fish vanish and canals flood. Different life and altitude sickness, so they are best settled in the lowland colonies or as coast traders.
Already living around the lake as low-status fishers. Equal treatment makes them loyal boat crews and fishery experts.
Quechua-speaking farmers on the road north. Similar ayllu life; a different language but long trade ties.
Terrace farmers and herders with a similar way of life, joining for roads and storehouses.
Forest peoples drawn by bronze tools and trade. Different language, food and climate; they stay in their valleys as trading partners.
Ash from a huge eruption in Ecuador ruins northern fields. Far away; few would reach the lake, but northern partners could take them in.

neighbors.d: A small kingdom with big ambitions and a royal family that claims descent from the sun and from Lake Titicaca. Delegations could come to learn; in real history they conquer the lake in the 1400s.
Warlike and expanding. Best brought in early by roads, trade and council seats before they grow strong in the 1300s–1400s.
Dense, fertile, divided into feuding hilltop towns. Easy to win with storehouse insurance, but far away.

neighbors.pop: ~30,000 in Chan Chan; ~300,000–500,000 in the kingdom (guess)
neighbors.d: The only real state in 1230: a king, nobles, canals and fine metalwork, expanding along the coast. Proud and rich; sits on the coal. The key partner, never an easy conquest.
Sea traders on balsa rafts who run the guano islands and the trade north to Ecuador. They want wool, metal and dried food.
Bronze-smelting lords of the far north coast, weakened after ~1100. The Chimú absorb them in the 1300s.
A northern highland valley tied to the Chimú. Where the Spanish captured the last Inca in 1532.
Caravan traders of the southern deserts, already linked to the altiplano since Tiwanaku. Guides to copper, salt and nitrates.
Lowland raised-field and causeway builders on the flooded plains east of the Andes. Malaria and distance keep them apart.
Ocean raft traders who sail for Spondylus shell and may reach Mexico by sea. The way out to the wider Americas, and the likely route for any Polynesian contact.
